transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what’s been bringing you here today?

Hi, yeah, thank you for seeing me. I, um... well, it's a bit hard to explain, but I've been having these issues lately. I work as a cashier, which, you know, isn't exactly what I pictured for myself at 42 when I got my bachelor's degree, and it can be pretty mentally draining. You're on your feet all day, dealing with all sorts of attitudes, just scanning things over and over. 

But anyway, what actually brought me in is that some nights after work, or sometimes if I've just had a really tense dinner, I'll go into the kitchen and I just... I start eating. And it's not like normal snacking where you just have a handful of something and walk away. It feels like the whole decision-making part of my brain just completely shuts off. It's the strangest, most frustrating thing because it's almost like I'm watching a movie of myself. I can literally see my own arm reaching into the pantry or the fridge for more food, and in my head, I'm fully aware of it, but I just can’t make myself stop. It’s like the brakes are completely cut and I'm just watching it happen without any say in the matter. I just keep reaching for more, and I don't know how to regain that control once it slips away like that. It just takes over entirely.
Can you tell me more about not being able to stop yourself from eating during those episodes? Does it feel like you're losing control completely, even though you’re aware of what you're doing?

Yeah, exactly. It's exactly like that. Like I was just saying a minute ago, it is a complete and total loss of control. It’s... well, it's kind of terrifying, honestly, because I'm a rational guy, right? I have a degree, I know how to think things through, but in those moments, it's like the logical part of my brain is trapped behind a glass wall. 

I can see what I'm doing. I can be standing there in the kitchen, maybe still in my work uniform, my feet throbbing from standing at the register for eight hours, and I'll have, I don't know, a whole box of crackers or whatever leftover takeout we had from that tense dinner I mentioned. And my brain is literally screaming at me, "What are you doing? Put it down. You're not even hungry, you don't even really want this." But my hands just keep going. They just keep unwrapping things, opening containers, bringing the food to my mouth. 

It's this incredibly bizarre disconnect where my physical body is completely ignoring my conscious mind. I mean, you'd think if you're fully aware of what you're doing, you could just say "stop" and that would be the end of it, right? But the brakes are just completely gone. It's like I'm a passenger in my own body. I try to mentally force myself to pull my hand back from the fridge, but it's like this overwhelming drive just overrides everything else. I just keep eating and eating, and I am entirely aware of how much I'm consuming the entire time, but the decision-making center that usually tells you "okay, you've had enough" is just completely unplugged from the rest of me. I really don't know how else to describe it other than being hijacked by my own self.
Do these episodes usually leave you feeling upset, guilty, or ashamed afterward, and have they affected your daily life or relationships in any way?

Oh, God, yes. The guilt is... it's heavy. It's so heavy. After it happens, after the, you know, the frenzy sort of dies down and I realize what I've just done, the shame just washes over me like a tidal wave. I just stand there looking at the wrappers or the empty containers, and I feel so disgusted with myself. I mean, I'm 42 years old, I should be able to control myself around a box of crackers or whatever it is, right? It just makes me feel so weak and pathetic, to be honest. 

And, you know, as for how it's affecting my life... well, I'm still going to work. I haven't missed any shifts at the store. I'm still standing there scanning groceries, smiling at the customers, doing what I need to do to pay the bills. I'm handling all my basic responsibilities, keeping the lights on, all of that. But... it's definitely bleeding into my personal life, especially with my family. 

I mentioned those tense dinners earlier... well, lately, I've just been avoiding them altogether when I can. If I know we're supposed to have a family meal, I'll make up an excuse. I'll say I'm too tired from work, or my feet are hurting too much, or I'll just kind of hide out in my room. Because if I do go, if I do sit down at the table with them, I'm not really *there*, you know? I'm completely distracted. My mind is just racing the whole time. I'm sitting there trying to make normal conversation, but in my head, I'm obsessing over what I ate the night before, or I'm panicking about what I'm eating right then, or... or I'm trying to figure out what I'm going to do later to fix it, to undo what I just did. So even when I am physically present, I'm just so wrapped up in my own head, worrying about the food and the guilt and the compensating for it, that I'm not really connecting with anyone. It's like this secret I'm carrying around, and it just puts this wall up between me and everyone else.
After these episodes of eating, do you ever make yourself sick, go on a fast, or exercise excessively to try to make up for what you've eaten?

Yeah... yeah, I do. It's... well, it's not something I'm proud of, obviously, and it's actually really hard to even say out loud, but yes. After it happens, after that whole out-of-body experience where I just consume everything in sight and that awful guilt sets in like I was talking about, I get this overwhelming panic. It's like this frantic need to just... erase it. To hit an undo button on the whole night. 

So, what happens is, I'll wait. I'll wait until the house is completely quiet, until I know for an absolute fact that everyone else is asleep and there's no chance of anyone walking in on me. I'll listen at the door, make sure the lights are out in the hallway, and then I'll go into the bathroom. I turn the fan on, sometimes I'll run the faucet just to be extra careful about the noise, and... I make myself throw up. I just lean over the toilet and force it all out. And in that moment, my brain is just repeating this loop, telling me, "It's fine, you're just undoing the damage, you're just fixing the mistake, it's just this once," even though I know it's not just this once. 

And if I don't do that, or sometimes even if I do, I'll resort to laxatives. I'll take them, again, just telling myself I'm clearing it all out, resetting the system, making up for what I did in the kitchen. But the thing is, it doesn't actually make me feel better. I mean, maybe for a split second there's a tiny bit of relief that the food is gone, but immediately after, I just feel so completely embarrassed. I'll be sitting there on the bathroom floor, my hands are usually shaking, my heart is racing, and I just feel so incredibly pathetic. I'm a grown man, you know? I shouldn't be hiding in my own bathroom in the middle of the night doing this to myself. It's just this vicious cycle of losing control, panicking, trying to purge it all away, and then feeling even worse, even more ashamed, when it's all over. It's exhausting, honestly. It's just so physically and mentally exhausting.
How often do these episodes of losing control while eating happen? Do they occur on a regular basis, and if so, how many times a week or month would you say this happens?

How often... well, it’s, I mean if I really sit down and think about it, looking back over the last few months... it’s been happening most weeks. I’d say almost every week I have at least one of those out-of-control eating nights. 

It usually builds up, you know? I’ll have a few days where I think, okay, I’m doing fine, I’m in control, I'm being a normal functioning adult, and then I’ll just hit a wall after a long shift and it all completely falls apart. And then, because I feel so awful about it, I spend the next day or two just desperately trying to make up for it. Like I said before, sometimes that means throwing up or taking laxatives that same night in the bathroom. But if I don't do that, or sometimes even if I do, I’ll try other things to sort of balance the scales, I guess. 

I’ll completely skip meals the next day. I'll wake up and just refuse to eat. I'll skip breakfast, work straight through my lunch break at the store, maybe just drink black coffee or water to get through my shift at the register, completely ignoring how empty or shaky I feel. Or I’ll force myself to go on a really long walk. And I mean a genuinely punishing walk. After standing on my feet for eight hours, when my heels are already throbbing and all I want to do is sit down and take my shoes off, I’ll just force myself to keep walking around the neighborhood for miles and miles. I'll just march around in the dark, trying to burn it off, trying to somehow walk off the guilt of what I ate. 

So, yeah, for the last few months, it's just been this exhausting weekly cycle. One bad night of losing control with the food, and then all this time spent punishing myself with the purging or the skipping meals or the walking. It just takes over my whole week, every single week, and it's so hard to break out of that loop once it starts.
Have these episodes or the behaviors you do afterward, like making yourself sick or skipping meals, affected your ability to function at work or in other areas of your life outside of family dinners?

Well, I know I kind of touched on this a few minutes ago, but to really give you the full picture... it’s this very strange sort of split existence I’m living right now. As far as the practical, day-to-day stuff goes, I’m still showing up for all my cashier shifts. I haven’t called out or missed any work because of this, which I guess is something I hold onto. I mean, I have my bachelor's degree, but right now I'm working the register, and I am there, physically doing the job. I’m handling my responsibilities, scanning the groceries, making sure my drawer balances at the end of the night, doing the small talk with the regulars who come in for their weekly shopping. I’m paying my bills and keeping a roof over my head. So, if you just looked at my attendance record at the store, you’d think everything was perfectly fine. 

But the reality is, even when I'm at work, my mind is just... it's somewhere else. I'll be bagging someone's apples, and internally I'm just obsessing over what I did the night before, or calculating exactly how long I need to go without eating to make up for it. 

And then outside of work, like I was saying about those family dinners... that's where it's really taking a toll. I’ve started actively avoiding them whenever I possibly can. I'll make up any excuse not to go. But when I can't get out of it, when I actually have to sit down at the table with them, I'm just acting so distracted. My mom or my sister will be talking right to me, telling me about their day, and I’m just nodding and giving these empty responses because I’m not really listening. My entire brain is just consumed with worrying about what I ate, or looking at the food on my plate and panicking, or planning out exactly what I’m going to do later in the bathroom to compensate for whatever I'm being forced to swallow right then. 

It’s like there’s this incredibly loud radio playing in my head all the time, broadcasting all my guilt and my plans to fix it, and it makes it impossible to just be a normal person having a normal dinner. So, yeah, I'm doing my job and I'm functioning on paper, but in terms of actually living my life and being present with my family... I'm just completely checked out. I'm just a prisoner to all this worry.
Do you find yourself overly preoccupied with your body shape or weight, to the point where it causes you significant distress or affects how you see yourself?

Oh, God, yes. It’s... honestly, it’s probably the thing that occupies my mind the most, aside from the food itself. It completely dictates how I feel about myself on any given day. Like, it’s so tied to my mood that it’s almost frightening. 

For instance, at work—we have these uniform shirts, these sort of stiff polos we have to wear at the grocery store. And they aren't the most flattering things to begin with, but... if I put that shirt on before my shift, and I feel it pulling, even just a fraction of an inch, right across my stomach? It just destroys my entire day. I’ll stand in my bedroom just pulling at it, trying to stretch the fabric, turning sideways in the mirror, just obsessing over it. And then I have to go in and stand at the register, and the whole time, for my entire eight-hour shift, I am just hyper-aware of how that shirt is fitting. 

Every time I reach across the scanner for a heavy item, or turn to hand someone their receipt, I feel the fabric pull, and I just... I spend the whole shift feeling like every single customer can see it. I get this horrible, sinking feeling that they’re staring at my stomach and thinking that I have absolutely no discipline. Like they can just see right through me, see all those nights I lost control, just broadcast right there on my waistline. 

And it’s exhausting because my entire mood, my whole sense of value as a person, just depends way, way too much on how I look that day. If I feel even slightly heavier, or if my clothes aren't hanging perfectly loose, I just feel completely worthless. I can't focus on anything else, I can't just brush it off and have a good day. I'll just be standing there ringing up groceries, smiling at people, while inside I'm just tearing myself apart over my shape. It just hangs over me like a dark cloud from the minute I wake up, and I can't seem to separate who I am from what I look like in the mirror.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences significant distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning specifically related to the eating disorder symptoms beyond the previously discussed family meals.
doctor.question: Have these episodes or the behaviors you do afterward, like making yourself sick or skipping meals, affected your ability to function at work or in other areas of your life outside of family dinners?

target_item.name: Functional Impairment
target_item.manifestation: I’m still showing up for my cashier shifts and handling my responsibilities, but I’ve started avoiding some family meals afterward or acting distracted because I’m worried about what I ate or what I’ll do to compensate.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking how the episodes and compensatory behaviors have affected my ability to function at work or in other areas of my life, which directly maps to the functional impairment profile.

patient.answer:
Well, I know I kind of touched on this a few minutes ago, but to really give you the full picture... it’s this very strange sort of split existence I’m living right now. As far as the practical, day-to-day stuff goes, I’m still showing up for all my cashier shifts. I haven’t called out or missed any work because of this, which I guess is something I hold onto. I mean, I have my bachelor's degree, but right now I'm working the register, and I am there, physically doing the job. I’m handling my responsibilities, scanning the groceries, making sure my drawer balances at the end of the night, doing the small talk with the regulars who come in for their weekly shopping. I’m paying my bills and keeping a roof over my head. So, if you just looked at my attendance record at the store, you’d think everything was perfectly fine. 

But the reality is, even when I'm at work, my mind is just... it's somewhere else. I'll be bagging someone's apples, and internally I'm just obsessing over what I did the night before, or calculating exactly how long I need to go without eating to make up for it. 

And then outside of work, like I was saying about those family dinners... that's where it's really taking a toll. I’ve started actively avoiding them whenever I possibly can. I'll make up any excuse not to go. But when I can't get out of it, when I actually have to sit down at the table with them, I'm just acting so distracted. My mom or my sister will be talking right to me, telling me about their day, and I’m just nodding and giving these empty responses because I’m not really listening. My entire brain is just consumed with worrying about what I ate, or looking at the food on my plate and panicking, or planning out exactly what I’m going to do later in the bathroom to compensate for whatever I'm being forced to swallow right then. 

It’s like there’s this incredibly loud radio playing in my head all the time, broadcasting all my guilt and my plans to fix it, and it makes it impossible to just be a normal person having a normal dinner. So, yeah, I'm doing my job and I'm functioning on paper, but in terms of actually living my life and being present with my family... I'm just completely checked out. I'm just a prisoner to all this worry.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient experiences distress or impairment in social, occupational, or other important areas of functioning due to body shape or weight concerns, which would support a diagnosis of an eating disorder such as anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa.
doctor.question: Do you find yourself overly preoccupied with your body shape or weight, to the point where it causes you significant distress or affects how you see yourself?

target_item.name: Body_Image_Weight_Shape_Disturbance
target_item.manifestation: When my cashier shirt pulls a little at my stomach, I spend the whole shift feeling like customers can tell I have no discipline, and my mood about myself depends way too much on how I look that day.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I am overly preoccupied with my body shape or weight and if it affects how I see myself, which directly matches the symptom of body weight or shape unduly influencing self-evaluation.

patient.answer:
Oh, God, yes. It’s... honestly, it’s probably the thing that occupies my mind the most, aside from the food itself. It completely dictates how I feel about myself on any given day. Like, it’s so tied to my mood that it’s almost frightening. 

For instance, at work—we have these uniform shirts, these sort of stiff polos we have to wear at the grocery store. And they aren't the most flattering things to begin with, but... if I put that shirt on before my shift, and I feel it pulling, even just a fraction of an inch, right across my stomach? It just destroys my entire day. I’ll stand in my bedroom just pulling at it, trying to stretch the fabric, turning sideways in the mirror, just obsessing over it. And then I have to go in and stand at the register, and the whole time, for my entire eight-hour shift, I am just hyper-aware of how that shirt is fitting. 

Every time I reach across the scanner for a heavy item, or turn to hand someone their receipt, I feel the fabric pull, and I just... I spend the whole shift feeling like every single customer can see it. I get this horrible, sinking feeling that they’re staring at my stomach and thinking that I have absolutely no discipline. Like they can just see right through me, see all those nights I lost control, just broadcast right there on my waistline. 

And it’s exhausting because my entire mood, my whole sense of value as a person, just depends way, way too much on how I look that day. If I feel even slightly heavier, or if my clothes aren't hanging perfectly loose, I just feel completely worthless. I can't focus on anything else, I can't just brush it off and have a good day. I'll just be standing there ringing up groceries, smiling at people, while inside I'm just tearing myself apart over my shape. It just hangs over me like a dark cloud from the minute I wake up, and I can't seem to separate who I am from what I look like in the mirror.

inference.note: This turn confirmed the presence of significant body image concerns and preoccupation with weight and shape, which supports eating disorder pathology. The patient's behaviors (binge eating followed by purging via vomiting/laxatives and excessive exercise) and the impact on functioning further align with anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa. Other candidates (F42.9, F32.9, F43.20, F19.10) are ruled out due to insufficient evidence for primary diagnosis of OCD, MDD, adjustment disorder, or other psychoactive substance use disorder).
